commentBody: Easy solve but I do not understand the theme.

Anagram-adjacent themes are not my effort, er I mean, forte, am I doing this right?

So instead, some less famous razors:

CROSSROAD’s razor: the tail-gater that you pull over to let pass will turn off at the very next crossroad.

GEORGE FOREMAN’s razor: the simplest solution is the correct one, i.e., name them all George.

Norman Reedus’ razor: for any obscure public figure, there is always another more obscure.
Did anybody else, besides me, confidently slap in SSNS for [Unshared numbers]?

So, first came the inspiration – finding actors’ names whose letters were in other famous people’s names.  That’s bringing letter-bank themes, which have been done before, to a new place.  Excellent idea!

Then came the grind – inputting hundreds of actor’s names into a program that found pairs of names that worked, and hoping to find names with letter counts that would make the answers symmetrical in the grid.

After that, came more inspiration, coming up with a punny revealer that landed perfectly.

Finally, more work – making it all work in a Sunday-sized grid.

Oh, I’m grateful, Daniel, for a fun romp through this puzzle, and I love how the theme not only helped fill in the theme answers, but it caused me to think in a different and fun way to get from the clue name to the answer name.

But I’m also grateful for all you put into the making of this. It sure paid off for me.  Thank you, sir!

I’ve always had the outspoken opinion that anagram themes need a reason for being beyond a catchy revealer. In other words; the anagrammed entries should have something to do with the clues. Otherwise it solves just like a themeless where you have no clues for some of the entries, since most people aren’t going to do the anagrams in their head. Maybe this meets me half way, since both clues and entries are celebrities. I still think that’s not quite enough, because there are so many names to pick from and they are otherwise unrelated. I think these were all pretty famous, at least, although SAL MINEO and ELAINE STRITCH are probably more in my wheelhouse than most. Then of course, this is a word bank, not an anagram, which decreases points for difficulty and the likelihood that people will use the letters to solve. Much less of a wow factor for me. So, all said and done, I would review this, based on solving enjoyment, as I would a themeless; and here we’re back to the sad fact that most Sundays are clued at a Tuesday level at best. For me this was just an exercise in filling in letters and if the across wasn’t a gimme the down usually was. Too bad, because the idea and the execution were still clever.
